opus-5.5.text:
For me, the most fundamental definition is pretty simple: a general robot brain is a single model that can take in what the robot sees, hears, and is told, and turn that into physical action across many tasks, many environments, and ideally many bodies, without being re-engineered for each one.

The key word is "general," and I'd break it into three parts.

The first is generality across tasks. Today most deployed robots are specialists. One system picks boxes, another folds laundry, and each one is its own project with its own data and its own tuning. A general brain should be able to fold laundry, wipe a table, and load a dishwasher, and when you give it a new instruction in natural language, it should make a reasonable attempt instead of failing completely.

The second is generality across environments. A robot that works in one lab, under one lighting setup, with one set of objects, isn't really general. The real test is whether you can drop it into a kitchen it has never seen, with clutter and unfamiliar objects, and still get useful behavior. That kind of robustness to the messiness of the real world is, I think, the hardest part.

The third, which people often overlook, is generality across embodiments. Ideally the same brain transfers across different arms, grippers, mobile bases, maybe even humanoids, the way a person can pick up a new tool and adapt quickly. If every new robot body requires starting from scratch, you don't really have a brain. You have a controller.

Underneath all of that, what really defines a robot brain, as opposed to a language model or a vision model, is that it has to close the loop with the physical world. It's not enough to describe what should happen. It has to act, see the consequences, and correct itself in real time. Physics doesn't let you hand-wave. If the grasp is off by a centimeter, the cup falls.

So if I had to compress it into one sentence: a general robot brain is a foundation model for physical action, something that understands the world well enough, and has enough embodied common sense, to do useful work in situations it was never explicitly trained for. We're not fully there yet, but over the last couple of years it has stopped feeling like science fiction and started feeling like an engineering and data problem. That shift is what makes this moment so exciting.

r001.rationale: The response says a general brain should transfer across different robot embodiments, such as arms, grippers, mobile bases, and humanoids, and treats this as one of its three dimensions of generality.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about it is this: a general robot brain, at its most fundamental, is a system that can take in perception from the physical world and produce physical actions to accomplish goals, and it can do this across different bodies, different environments, and different tasks without being redesigned for each one.

If you strip away all the technical layers, there are really two things that matter. The first is understanding. The brain has to perceive the world, not just as pixels or point clouds, but as objects, relationships, and consequences. It has to know that a cup is something you can grasp, that it will spill if tilted, that the person reaching toward it probably wants it. That is world knowledge grounded in physics and in human intention. The second is action. Understanding alone is not a robot brain; a language model that can describe how to fold laundry is not a robot brain. The brain has to close the loop. It has to translate understanding into motor commands, observe the result, and correct in real time.

What makes it "general" rather than just a robot controller is that the same underlying model handles the long tail. Historically, every robot in a factory was programmed for one task, in one fixed setup, and if you moved the conveyor belt ten centimeters, everything broke. A general brain is the opposite. You can put it in a kitchen it has never seen, give it an instruction it has never heard phrased that way, and it still produces reasonable behavior. Generality is really about transfer, across tasks, across embodiments, and across environments.

I would add one more piece that I think people underrate. A general robot brain has to be able to learn from experience in the world, not just from a static dataset. Language models learned from the internet because the internet already existed. There is no internet of physical interaction. So the brain itself has to be the thing that generates and absorbs that data, through teleoperation, through simulation, through its own trial and error. Any definition that leaves out learning is describing a very sophisticated but ultimately brittle controller.

So in one sentence: it is a perception-to-action model with grounded world knowledge, that transfers across bodies and tasks, and that keeps improving from physical experience. Everything else, the architecture, the training recipe, the hardware, is a means to that end.

r001.rationale: The response defines a general robot brain as one system that works across different bodies and explicitly says it transfers across embodiments.

astra-6.text:
I think the most fundamental definition is a brain that can generalize beyond the specific tasks it was trained to do. You can give the robot a goal, and it can understand its surroundings, figure out how to act, and adjust based on what actually happens.

The key is that you shouldn’t need to build a new system for every task or every environment. If you move the robot into an unfamiliar room or give it an object it hasn’t seen before, it should be able to use what it already knows, learn what’s different, and make progress. That ability to transfer knowledge and adapt is what makes the brain general.

r001.rationale: The response describes generalizing across tasks and environments, but does not identify controlling robots with different physical configurations as a requirement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most fundamental definition is a system that can turn a general intention into action in the physical world. You give it a goal, and it can understand its surroundings, decide what to do, execute those actions, and adjust based on what actually happens.

The key word is “general.” If every new task or environment requires us to write another program, then we still have a collection of specialized systems. A general robot brain should be able to carry what it has learned into unfamiliar situations, learn new skills, and recognize when it needs help. It doesn’t have to do everything perfectly, but it needs a common foundation for learning and acting across different tasks.

r001.rationale: The response describes acting across different tasks and unfamiliar environments, but does not identify controlling robots with different physical configurations as the fundamental requirement.
